Rapid growth of the population will accentuate this problem in the future, in the absence of substantial new employment opportunities. A careful examination of the economic base of southeast Montana shows no likely sources of substantial numbers of new basic jobs, except those directly or indirectly associated with coal development.
2. Development of Crow coal would create a large number of jobs. Even more importantly, a relatively large proportion of the jobs could be filled by Crows if they were available for work and if they have or can acquire the necessary skills.
3. The lower the level of development, or the higher the labor force participation rates of the area's residents, the smaller will be in-migration into the impact area. Similarly, the higher the level of Crow participation, the lower will be non-Crow employment levels.
4. The population of Reservation towns is not likely to be much affected by any isolated Westmoreland Resources activity. However, simultaneous development of nearby coal leases (such as the Shell Oil Company or Gulf Oil Company lease tracts to the south on the Reservation) could cause very important impacts to be felt in the southeastern part of the impact area.
5. The incremental effect on Hardin of combining Westmoreland's most probable level of development (Scenario 1) with substantial other coal development in the region (AF-2) could be highly significant.
